source.title: Progressive Scaling Visual Object Tracking
source.authors: Jack Hong; Shi-Lin Yan; Ze-Hao Xiao; Jia-Yin Cai; Xiao-Long Jiang; Yao Hu; Henghui Ding

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table formatting is flattened, but the relevant Table 3 mean-AUC values are legible.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling analysis to visual object tracking and reports tracking performance as training data, model size, and input resolution are scaled. It does not test language-model cross-entropy scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper reports tracking accuracy, not held-out language-model loss, power-law fits, or extrapolation from small runs. Results about the proposed DT-Training method, compression, multimodal tracking, object detection, and comparisons with other trackers are not rows for these claim versions. Table 2 values are used only where their model/metric alignment is clear.
record.test_reason: This is a visual-tracking methods paper. Its scaling results are tracking AUC at two or three points per factor (ViT-B/L/H, normal vs 4x data, 256 vs 384 resolution). It fits no power law or other functional form, reports no loss, and tests no extrapolation or compute-optimal split. Most headline numbers (Tables 2–4) compare its own DT-Training against naive training. The pioneer results show accuracy rising with diminishing returns. That is related to, but not, any version: V5 needs the power-law form in a new setting, and V6 concerns predictable downstream gains for language-model-style scaling. No version is tested, so the record's V6 labels are dropped.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find that scaling model size, data and resolution consistently improves tracking, with diminishing returns under naive training, which they attribute to optimization limits. Their DT-Training (small-teacher transfer plus masked dual-branch alignment) yields larger gains, state-of-the-art 64.8 mean AUC on their GTrack Bench, and transfers to compression, multimodal tracking and object detection (+1.5 AP).
record.recipe_differences: This is a visual-tracking scaling study using tracking AUC and benchmark performance, not a language-model held-out cross-entropy study or a reproduction of the original LM scaling methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports diminishing gains at larger model sizes and says mask ratio and regularization parameters affect DT-Training performance; those DT-Training ablations do not test the scaling-law versions here.

fits_no_version.finding: With naive training of OSTrack, tracking AUC rises with model size (ViT-B→L), training data (4 datasets→4x) and input resolution (256→384). Gains diminish: ViT-L→ViT-H gives +0.3 mean AUC, and data gains slow. The authors attribute the slowdown to the training method rather than to a scaling limit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In fine-tuned vision trackers, accuracy improves monotonically but with diminishing returns as model size, data and resolution grow, and the attainable gain depends on the training procedure.

record.problems: No language-model losses, power-law fits, extrapolation tests, or compute-optimal allocation experiments are reported. The GTrack Bench progressive comparisons also change the training method, so their gains cannot be attributed to scaling alone. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 benchmark-specific AUC values are omitted because the table also provides aggregate mean AUC results for the same configurations; SOTA comparisons and DT-Training ablations are not direct tests of V6 scaling behavior. Table 2 values beyond the clearly aligned LaSOT AUC comparisons are omitted because the flattened layout makes assignment of all metric entries uncertain.

untested.parts: Power-law form in vision tracking: no functional form is fitted to the scaling curves.
Predictability of downstream gains from scale or loss: only a few ordinal comparisons are given, with no predictive fit.

missing.what: Pioneer scaling curves for model size, data volume and resolution, varying one factor at a time. Values are not legible in the text; these are the only multi-point scaling data in the paper.
missing.versions: none (would be needed for any V5 power-law assessment)

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses 'scaling law' loosely to mean 'performance improves with scale'; it never fits a law. Table 3 baselines are naive training at each scale, so Ours-vs-Baseline gaps measure DT-Training, not scaling. All record rows are relinked to none and the record's V6 supports/limits_scope labels are removed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss and power-law relationships with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Fitting power laws on small runs and predicting substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its trend with compute.
Controlled comparisons of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
The study reports downstream tracking performance under scaling, but does not predict downstream results from pretraining loss or fit a predictive scaling function.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and systematic departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: Baseline-B-256-M
rows.operation_detail: Increased training data volume from the usual four tracking datasets to the expanded set.
rows.note: The reported LaSOT AUC rises slightly with the expanded data condition.
rows.check: Two-point data comparison (68.4→68.6 LaSOT AUC) for a vision tracker. It fits no functional form, so it cannot show power-law behaviour (V5) or predictability (V6).

rows.subject: Baseline-L-256-N
rows.stage_stated: trained on the usual four tracking datasets
rows.operation_detail: Compared the larger ViT-L model with the ViT-B model while keeping resolution and training-data condition fixed.
rows.note: The comparison changes model size while retaining the stated data and resolution conditions.
rows.check: Two-point ViT-B→ViT-L comparison (68.4→70.0). It shows a gain but no scaling law; it does not bear on any version's power-law or predictability claim.

rows.subject: Baseline-B-384-N
rows.stage_stated: trained on the usual four tracking datasets
rows.note: This is an input-resolution comparison, not a parameter/token/compute scaling result.
rows.check: Input-resolution change (256→384), which is not a parameter, token or compute axis named by any version.

rows.subject: Ours-B-256-M
rows.stage_stated: trained with DT-Training on expanded training data
rows.operation_detail: Progressively scaled the training data condition; the reported run also uses DT-Training.
rows.note: The paper reports this aggregate mean across the benchmarks in GTrack Bench; the comparison also changes the training method.
rows.check: Confounded: it compares Ours (DT-Training, more data) with the naive baseline. This is the study's own method against a baseline, not a scaling result; it should not be a scaling row.

rows.subject: Ours-L-256-M
rows.stage_stated: trained with DT-Training on expanded training data
rows.operation_detail: Used the larger model and expanded data condition in the progressive-scaling comparison.
rows.note: The paper reports this aggregate mean across the benchmarks in GTrack Bench; the comparison also changes the training method.
rows.check: Confounded by the training method (Ours-L-256-M vs Baseline-L-256-N); it compares the study's own method with a baseline.

rows.subject: Ours-L-384-M
rows.stage_stated: trained with DT-Training on expanded training data
rows.operation_detail: Used the largest reported progressive-scaling configuration, with increased data, model size, and input resolution.
rows.note: The paper reports this aggregate mean across the benchmarks in GTrack Bench; the comparison also changes the training method.
rows.check: Confounded by the training method (Ours-L-384-M vs Baseline-L-384-N); it compares the study's own method with a baseline.

rows.subject: OSTrack ViT-H
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean AUC after increasing the backbone from ViT-L to ViT-H.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a less noticeable gain from further model-size expansion.
rows.check: Text-only report of a 0.3% mean-AUC gain from ViT-L to ViT-H. It indicates diminishing returns but fits no curve, so it cannot show departure from or adherence to a power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
